title: Tenali Raman and the Magic Mirror of Honesty

full_text:
A chest containing ten thousand silver coins disappeared from the imperial tax registry office in Vijayanagara.
The Chief Treasurer suspected that one of his four senior accountants had embezzled the funds, but having no proof, could not identify the culprit.
He appealed to Tenali Raman.

Tenali had the four accountants brought into a darkened chamber in the palace.
In the center of the room stood an ornate bronze mirror covered with a dark velvet cloth.
Tenali announced with solemn gravity:
'Brothers, this is the ancient Celestial Mirror of Truth, blessed by Himalayan hermits.
It has a miraculous power:
Each of you must step into this dark room alone, pull aside the cloth, look directly into the glass, and strike the surface gently with your palm.
If you are innocent, the mirror will remain silent and smooth.
But if you are the thief who stole the silver, the mirror will immediately emit a deafening, thunderous roar that will shake the citadel, and your face will turn permanently black in the glass!'

The four accountants listened with beating hearts.
Before the test began, Tenali had privately coated the bronze surface of the mirror with a thick, odorless layer of sticky black lamp-soot!

One by one, the four accountants entered the dark room alone, completed the test, and emerged into the bright audience hall.

Tenali called the four men forward:
'Now, hold up both your palms before His Majesty!'

The first three accountants, whose consciences were completely clear, held up their palms:
Both their palms were coated in thick, black lamp-soot, because they had fearlessly touched the mirror without hesitation!

Then the fourth accountant, a man named Narahari, held up his hands:
His palms were completely, spotlessly clean and white!

Tenali grasped Narahari’s wrist and shouted:
'Behold the thief!'

Narahari trembled in shock: 'What? My hands are clean! How can I be the thief?'

Tenali explained with brilliant psychological logic:
'Thy hands are clean because thy conscience was guilty!
Thou wert so terrified that the mirror would roar and turn thy face black that thou didst not dare touch the glass at all!
The three innocent men touched the mirror without fear, knowing their innocence, and received the soot.
Thou alone didst keep thy hands in thy pockets!'

Narahari broke down in tears, confessed his embezzlement, and revealed where the ten thousand silver coins were hidden beneath his stable floor.
King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s psychological mastery, proving that an innocent heart fears no test, while guilt betrays itself by its own cowardice.
moral: Guilt makes cowards of us all; those who fear the reflection of truth expose their own dishonesty.
